council.name: Norwich City Council
council.remit_note: Norwich City Council is a district council with city status. In Norfolk, local government is split between two councils, and Norwich does the half you meet day to day: the council housing it owns and manages itself, bin collections, parks, planning applications, and licensing — who may sell alcohol, put on entertainment, or serve hot food and drink late at night. Roads and potholes, schools and libraries, and social care for children and adults belong to Norfolk County Council instead, so you will not find those here.

topic.name: Housing allocations
topic.plain_english: The rules Norwich City Council follows when it decides who can join the waiting list for a council or housing association home in the city, and who gets offered one first. The scheme is called Home Options. It does not produce any more homes — in the council's words, it is “a fairer, more efficient and transparent way of allocating the social housing available”.

questions.asked: People were asked what they thought of five changes to who can join Norwich's housing register and who is offered a home first: telling applicants with no priority band that they are unlikely to be rehoused and pointing them elsewhere; raising the local connection rule from six months' residence in Norwich to two years; cutting the number of offers you may refuse from five to three; setting out when someone sleeping rough is given silver band; and offering a home to a UK armed forces veteran ahead of others in the same band. Seventy-two responses came in. Agreement ran from 71 per cent on the first change down to 37 per cent on veterans' priority, which 43 per cent were neutral about; the local connection change was the one most people objected to, at 26 per cent against.
questions.decided: Two meetings. On 15 January 2026 the Scrutiny committee suggested no changes to the five proposals, then by a majority vote asked Cabinet to consider deleting a sixth thing nobody had proposed changing: paragraph 3.8.7.3, which withholds that extra priority where the children were already born when the family accepted the property. On 11 February 2026 Cabinet adopted the updated policy with all five changes, and refused the Scrutiny request — the report says it “has been considered by the Portfolio Holder but is not accepted”. The council says the consultation changed three things in its proposal: how it assesses the needs of someone sleeping rough, the wording on decisions being based on evidence rather than opinion, and how it treats rent arrears caused by financial abuse. All three can be seen in the adopted scheme.
questions.done: The rules themselves are finished. The Home Options Allocation Scheme 2026 was published on 12 February 2026, the day after Cabinet agreed it, and it is the scheme the council applies now — its own page for applicants states the two-year residence rule the new scheme introduced. What we cannot tell you is what it has changed in practice. The council said the consultation responses “will be published, along with council comments, in an online report”; a consultation report was published for the homelessness strategy the same survey covered, but not for the allocations half, so what people wrote about these five changes is still unpublished. Nothing published says how many applicants the two-year rule has kept off the register. On effect, we are still waiting.

sources.title: Homelessness Strategy and Housing Allocations Policy — consultation (Get Talking Norwich)

It says the consultation was open “from Monday 10 November 2025 to Sunday 7 December 2025”, and offers a draft policy, a briefing note and an equality impact assessment to read before answering the survey. Since it closed the council has added a “you said, we did” update naming what it changed in the allocations proposal because of what people said. sources.title: Allocations policy 2025 - consultation draft
sources.summary: The full draft allocations scheme as residents saw it during the consultation, and the longest document in this archive. It sets out who could join the register, the five priority bands, how homes are advertised and bid for, and how to challenge a decision, including the exception that lets someone keep priority despite rent arrears “where a person is fleeing violence and has rent arrears”. Because the council later published the adopted version in the same form, this draft is what makes it possible to see which wording moved and which did not.

sources.title: Allocations Policy 2025 – Equality Impact Assessment

events.title: The council asked what people thought of five changes to who gets a council home
events.summary: Norwich put five proposed changes to its Home Options allocations scheme out to public consultation on Get Talking Norwich, alongside a new homelessness strategy. The page told people it was open “from Monday 10 November 2025 to Sunday 7 December 2025” and offered a draft policy, a briefing note and an equality impact assessment to read first. Seventy-two responses came in. After it closed the council published a “you said, we did” update naming what it had changed in the allocations proposal as a result.
detail: The five changes: a conversation with an adviser for every applicant, with those who do not qualify for a priority band told plainly that they are unlikely to be rehoused; two years' continuous residence in Norwich instead of six months; three permitted refusals instead of five; a written rule on when a rough sleeper is given silver band; and UK armed forces veterans offered a home ahead of others in the same band.

The council's own account of what it changed: “Following feedback from the public and partners, and in line with the new national homelessness strategy, we have updated how we assess the needs of people sleeping rough. This includes using a personalised needs assessment. Silver banding will only be offered when no other off‑the‑street accommodation is available.”

Two council documents give different closing dates. The consultation page says Sunday 7 December 2025; the report to Cabinet says the consultation took place “between 10 November and 12 December 2025”. Both are the council's own words, so we give both rather than pick one.

What individual people wrote has not been published and is not shown here. The only response figures the council released are the agree, disagree and neutral percentages for each of the five proposals.

events.title: Scrutiny committee asked Cabinet to delete the exception to the no-garden rule
events.summary: The Scrutiny committee took the proposals on 15 January 2026. Officers told members the changes had been consulted on and that 72 responses had been received. The committee suggested no changes to the five proposals. It then went beyond what the report asked and, by a majority vote, resolved to “ask Cabinet to consider removing paragraph 3.8.7.3 from the proposed policy” — a rule already in the scheme, and not one of the changes officers had put forward. Deleting it would have widened who gets the extra priority, not narrowed it.
detail: Paragraph 3.8.7 gives silver band to a household with a child aged ten or under living in a flat or maisonette with no garden or private outdoor space. Paragraph 3.8.7.3 takes it back where the children were already born at the point the family accepted that property.

The minutes record that “Several Members stated that the line in the policy was poorly worded”, and that earlier in the discussion a member was “concerned housing arrangements did not facilitate shared custody of children and that children would be penalised for their parents' decision making”.

The committee noted two further actions. It asked for more about the council's assessment panel — “the make up of the panel, its governance and decision-making processes” — to be written into the policy, and for officers to look for research on the effect of co-parenting in council-owned properties and report back at a later meeting.

A member also asked whether the “honest and realistic conversations” the housing team has with applicants are guided by trauma-informed care practices. Officers said the council was part of a trauma-informed practice working group and took a person-centred approach.

Officers were asked which changes the law required. The minutes record that “the addition of the realistic conversation and the reduction in number of refusals were Council additions, and the remaining changes were due to guidance and legislation”.

events.title: Cabinet adopted the updated scheme, and turned down Scrutiny's request
events.summary: Cabinet met on 11 February 2026 and, as item 12, “RESOLVED to agree the adoption of the updated Home Options policy.” All five proposed changes went through. The one thing Scrutiny had asked for did not. The report records that the recommendation to remove section 3.8.7.3 “has been considered by the Portfolio Holder but is not accepted”, and the Cabinet member for housing told the meeting that these are households who “made an active choice to move to a property without a garden”. The question that prompted that answer had put the other side: a councillor asked what the council would do so the rule did not work against children, since “this is clearly not the children's decision”.
detail: An applicant now has to have lived in Norwich for two years to join the register, rather than six months, with the exceptions set out in law still applying.

After three refused offers — or three viewings missed without good cause — the council reviews the application and the band. If a team leader or manager decides the refusals were unreasonable or without grounds, the application is cancelled and no new one is accepted for at least twelve months. People the council owes a homelessness duty still get a single offer, as the law requires.

Two other concerns raised in the consultation were answered rather than acted on. The report says that people without a local connection staying longer in hostels is covered by the council's hostel move-on agreement, and that prioritising veterans follows the Armed Forces Covenant, which the council has signed.

Cabinet pointed families in a flat with no garden towards swapping homes with another tenant instead, and gave a figure for how often that works — “in 2025 alone, 160 council tenant households were able to move through this process”.

events.title: The new scheme was published the next day
events.summary: The Home Options Allocation Scheme 2026 went up on the council's website on 12 February 2026, the day after Cabinet agreed it, as a full web page rather than a download. Its opening summary says the updates “have been shaped through a public consultation which took place in Autumn 2025 and scrutiny by the council's Overview and Scrutiny Committee.”
detail: You can see the consultation in the text. The words “needs-led” and “professional judgement” appear nowhere in the draft that went out for consultation. Both appear twice in the adopted scheme: in the summary of changes at the top, and in the rough sleeping section itself. The draft's promise that rough sleeping priority would be “subject to ongoing, regular verification” is not in the adopted scheme.

The council said it had “updated our policy wording to make it clear that housing application decisions are based on objective evidence rather than opinion”. Neither document uses the phrase “objective evidence”, but the change is there. The clause on behaviour dropped “a history of behaviour which, in the opinion of the council, is unacceptable” for “a history of behaviour which is evidenced to have caused a detrimental effect to others”, and “in the opinion of” appears nowhere in the adopted scheme. One judgement of the council's does survive a few lines later, on rent arrears “which, in the council's view, would entitle the landlord to a possession order”.

One more line moved, and the council says why. The scheme gives reduced preference to people who owe housing debts, with exceptions. The draft made an exception “where a person is fleeing violence and has rent arrears”; the adopted scheme makes it “where a person is fleeing violence or domestic abuse and has rent arrears”. The council's own update says it changed how the policy refers to rent arrears caused by financial abuse, “to ensure survivors are not unfairly prevented from joining the housing register when they need support”.
Section 3.8.7.3 is still in the scheme, as “This category will not be awarded to those households whose children were born when the current accommodation was accepted.”

events.title: The new rules are the ones you meet when you apply
events.summary: The council's page for people looking for a council home now sets out the rules the 2026 scheme brought in. It tells applicants they can apply if they are 18 or older and “you've lived in Norwich for at least 2 years” — the requirement that replaced six months — lists the five bands an application can be placed in, and links the adopted scheme. This is the difference between a policy that was agreed and a policy that is being used.
detail: The five bands, in the council's own order: emergency for urgent issues such as unsafe housing or serious medical needs; gold for high priority such as risk of homelessness; silver for medium needs; bronze for lower priority or no local connection; standard for everyone else.
The page carries no date, so we cannot say when it was changed.

events.title: What the changes have done has not been published
events.summary: The scheme has been in force since February 2026 and nothing the council has published says what it has changed: not how many applicants the two-year residence rule has kept off the register, and not how many people sleeping rough have been given silver band under the new needs-led assessment. The scheme says it “will be monitored directly by the Housing Options manager”, weighing application and bidding data and feedback from applicants, but it does not promise to publish any of it.
detail: The council also told Cabinet that the consultation responses “will be published, along with council comments, in an online report”. A public consultation report was published for the homelessness strategy the survey covered at the same time — it is on the consultation page and in the Cabinet papers — but no equivalent report for the allocations proposals has appeared.

The equality assessment sets a date. It says the impact of the policy will be reviewed a year after it started, in February 2027. Nothing from that review has been published, and it is the first thing worth looking for.

measures.question: Is the council collecting the rent its tenants owe?
measures.label: Council housing rent collected, excluding old arrears, Q1 2025/26
measures.rule: Green if the council's reported figure met or beat the target it set itself. Amber if it missed the target but stayed on the safe side of the council's own intervention level — the point at which the council says it will step in and act. Red if it crossed that line. Grey if the council has not published a target, an intervention level, or the figure.
measures.council_caveat: The council's own explanation: "Cash collection in quarter one dropped compared to 2024/25, mainly due to the rise in Universal Credit (UC) claimants—now 55% of tenants. This shift reduced Housing Benefit payments by £1.5 million, with UC managed payments leaving a £110,000 gap… Rising living costs are worsening tenant finances." The council publishes these numbers as screenshots of a dashboard inside a PDF, so they cannot be read by machine. We read them off the images by eye, which is why this measure is flagged for human checking.
measures.evidence: Rent from council tenants pays for repairs, new homes and the debt on the existing ones, so a shortfall matters to every tenant. The council's own title for this indicator is "% of council housing rent collected (excluding arrears brought forward)", so unlike the council tax figure on this page it counts only the year's own rent. It aims to collect 99.8% and says it will step in below 98.8%. In the first quarter of 2025/26 it collected 96.88%.

gaps.description: A single closing date for the consultation. The consultation page says it ran to Sunday 7 December 2025 and the adopted scheme repeats that date; the report to Cabinet says the consultation took place “between 10 November and 12 December 2025”. Both are the council's own words and we have no record that resolves them, so we show both.

The consultation report for the allocations half. The report to Cabinet says the responses “will be published, along with council comments, in an online report”. For the homelessness strategy that happened: a public consultation report sits on the consultation page as Appendix A, and in the Cabinet papers as Annex D to the strategy report taken the same evening. For Home Options there is no equivalent. What has been published for it is the agree / disagree / neutral percentages in Appendix C and the council's short “you said, we did” note. What people actually wrote is still unpublished.

An equality assessment of the policy that was actually adopted. The one in the papers was completed on 4 November 2025, before the consultation opened, and it assesses the version that went out to consultation. Officers then changed the rough sleeping proposal in response to what people said, and no revised assessment of the changed version has been published. The assessment does commit the council to reviewing the policy's impact a year after it started, in February 2027.

How the council's assessment panel decides. The Scrutiny committee asked for “the make up of the panel, its governance and decision-making processes” to be written into the policy, and “Officers agreed to provide that information within the policy”. Part of that happened: the adopted scheme says the panel is “made up of Housing Options team leaders and/or managers”, which the consultation draft did not. But the scheme leaves decisions on medical need, exceptional circumstances and household composition to that panel in fourteen places, and nowhere sets out its governance or how it reaches a decision.

The decision that adopted the scheme this one replaced. Both the briefing note and the Cabinet report say the previous Home Options policy dates from October 2021, but neither links the meeting that agreed it, and the committee records we hold for this topic start in January 2026.

The research on co-parenting the Scrutiny committee asked for. Officers agreed to look for research on the effect of co-parenting in council-owned properties and “provide a brief update at a future Scrutiny Committee meeting”. We have not gathered any Scrutiny papers later than January 2026, so we cannot say whether that update has happened.

A published target for the allocations scheme itself. The council measures how long a home stands empty and how much rent it collects, but nothing it publishes sets a target for how long someone waits on the housing register, how many people move out of each priority band, or what the two-year residence rule introduced in 2026 has done to the register. The scheme's own equality assessment commits the council to reviewing its impact in February 2027.

A target for anything tenants are asked about. The Regulator of Social Housing makes every landlord publish a set of tenant satisfaction measures, and Norwich publishes 22 of them on this page: 75.3% of tenants satisfied with the overall service, up from 71.1%, and 30.0% satisfied with how complaints are handled. But the regulator does not require a target and Norwich has not set one, so none of them can be scored. A figure with nothing to compare it against is a figure, not a verdict, and we will not invent the standard.

Housing performance figures in a form anyone can check. The council's quarterly report carries a target, an intervention level and an actual for each housing indicator. The numbers themselves are screenshots of a dashboard pasted into a PDF, so they cannot be searched or checked by machine. Everything on this page taken from them was read off the images by eye and is flagged for human checking.

Numbers showing what the new rules have done. Nothing published says how many applicants the two-year residence rule has kept off the register, how many applications have been cancelled after three refusals, or how many people sleeping rough have been placed in silver band under the needs-led assessment. The scheme puts monitoring in the hands of the Housing Options manager without promising to publish what it finds. The equality assessment goes further and commits the council to reviewing the policy's impact a year after it started, in February 2027. Nothing from that review has appeared yet.

The allocation scheme at the address the council's own report links to. Paragraph 2 of the report to Cabinet names the current scheme as a hyperlink to www.norwich.gov.uk/your-council-explained/policies-plans-and-strategies/norwich-home-options-allocation-scheme. Followed on 7 September 2026, that address refused us with “Access denied”. The scheme is readable at the address used throughout this page, so nothing is lost — but a council report pointing residents at a page they cannot open is worth recording, and the address is given here so anyone can check it.

Why some of the council's own indicators are not on this page. Its quarter one 2025/26 report says "There are 20 quarterly KPIs reported for this period" and its totals table counts 19, alongside a handful of annual indicators reported once a year. This site carries eighteen of them, picked because each answers a question about money, about a target the council set itself, or about a service a resident uses. Eight are on the same dashboard and are not here: household waste recycled, food premises inspected, planning appeals, planning applications decided in time, underused council land, CO2 reduction, and two on IT availability. We have not published a rule for that choice, so the count of greens, ambers and reds on this page cannot be set against the council's own count. The council also says of every one of these indicators that "The KPIs in this report have been carried over from the previous Corporate Plan and are under review, as part of the new business planning process."

How many people are on Norwich's housing register, and how that has moved. The consultation page says around 4,000 people are waiting for social housing and that the council takes over 1,200 housing enquiries a month, but gives no date and no source for either, and we found no published register statistics to check them against.
